## The change

Read these before touching code (all in your worktree unless absolute):
- `app/docs/architecture/estados-de-encuestas-y-sesiones.md` (the main note: the featured session as a mark, its rules, the home and admin screens), and the notes it links: `modelo-de-datos.md`, `invariantes.md`, `acceso-a-datos.md`, `tiempo-real-del-aula.md`, `novedades-por-mail.md`, `carga-y-acciones-de-la-web.md`, `feedback-de-sesion.md`.
- The program design: /home/agus/workspace/filadd/agentic-engineering-famaf-extension-course/.scratch/preguntas-en-la-card/program-design/kurasu.md. Its eight branches and the Standards section name every type, function, component and file the change adds or touches, with the decisions Q1–Q3. Follow it. Where it and the notes disagree, the program design wins (its "Cambios a la fuente" section lists those points; the notes were already updated in `d09d518`).
- The design tree: /home/agus/workspace/filadd/agentic-engineering-famaf-extension-course/.scratch/preguntas-en-la-card/design.md.
- The prototypes, which settle how the screens look and behave, not how they are coded: `app/docs/prototipos/inicio-responsive.html` (student home), `app/docs/prototipos/admin-sesion.html` (session admin: Destacada switch, enable modal, confirmations, Preguntas destacadas, Activar) and `app/docs/prototipos/admin-sesiones.html` (teacher session list).

Summary. Today the featured session is derived (the last enabled one). It becomes an explicit mark the teacher sets: `sessions.featured` and `sessions.featured_questions` (migration `0004_featured_session`, booleans default false, a partial unique index so at most one session is featured). `SessionSummary` and `SessionChange` gain `featured` and `featuredQuestions`. Only the featured session accepts student writes (voting on a poll, asking, voting and deleting a question, raising and lowering a hand): elsewhere they keep today's 404 (`PollNotFound`/`QuestionNotFound`/`SessionNotFound`), through one `featuredSession` check that replaces `visibleSession` in those writes. Activating a poll or turning on featured questions outside the featured session answers a new `NotFeatured` (409). Featuring a session that would stay disabled answers `SessionDisabled`. When a session stops being featured (because another one is featured, the mark is removed, or it is disabled), its active polls close, its raised hands are lowered and its featured questions turn off, all in one D1 batch with the session change: `Sessions.update` reads the leaving session's active poll ids, then runs `Batch.run([sessions.writes.update(leaving, {featured:false, featuredQuestions:false}), polls.writes.updateWhere(ids, {status: closed}) (omitted when empty), hands.writes.removeWhere({sessionId}), sessions.writes.update(id, change)])`; `Repository.writes` is the deferred version of the write methods (opaque `Write`), built in `repositoryOf` from the `statements` it already has; the new core port `Batch` (`core/src/batch.ts`) has the adapter `D1Batch` (`database/src/batch.ts`), wired in `worker.ts`. The leaving session's classroom gets `session`, `polls` and `hands` notices, and its changelog items are removed. Turning featured questions on creates the new changelog item `questions-opened`; turning them off removes it. The first vote on a poll no longer removes `poll-opened`. `GET /api/classroom` enters the marked session; with no featured session nobody enters. The announcement mail links the featured session to `/` and the others to `/?sesion=<id>` (unchanged), and names "Preguntas abiertas" when they are on.

Web: the student home shows the featured card (`HighlightedSession` → `FeaturedSession`) with active polls of the featured session only and, when featured questions are on, a questions panel (`FeaturedQuestions`: the three most voted plus the student's own, "Mostrar N preguntas más" / "Mostrar menos", reusing `QuestionForm`, `QuestionList` with `emptyText`, `VoteToggle`, `DeleteOwnQuestion`). The list below is always titled "Todas las sesiones" (`EarlierSessions` → `AllSessions`) and includes the featured one, whose node is a star on red; no node shows a number; the featured card in the list shows "Entrar al aula"; `?sesion=<id>` of the featured session opens its card in the list. `railLook` (done/live/later) in `rail-look.ts` is shared by home and admin; `icons.ts` adds "star" (26px in the 44px node, 20px in the 32px mobile node). `/aula` takes the featured session by the mark. Admin of a session: `FeaturedSwitch`, `EnableSessionDialog` (narrow `Sheet`, opened when enabling), confirmations through `ConfirmDialog` (new `content` slot and `confirmIcon`) with `FeaturedEffects` counting active polls and raised hands via `useAdminPolls`/`useAdminRaisedHands`; `ContentTab` gets the featured session once via `useFeaturedSession` (`useAdminSessions({...options, select: findFeatured})`, module-level select) and passes it to `EnabledSwitch` and `FeaturedSwitch`; dialogs name the other featured session by title; "Sesión N de M" goes away (hero and Contenido card); `useUpdateSession` applies no optimistic patch for the waiting changes and invalidates sessions, adminSessions, adminChangelog, allAdminPolls and allAdminRaisedHands; `FeaturedQuestionsSwitch` is instant with a patch. Teacher list: `AdminHighlighted` → `AdminFeatured`, no chip, star on the featured node, disabled = empty dashed node, no numbers; `SessionLinks` prop `highlighted` → `featured`; `FeaturedLabel` is dropped. `PollStateActions` gets `isFeatured` (from the route) and hides Activar outside the featured session.

Out of scope: anything not in the program design; the mail link stays as it is.

## The tasks

They live in Entire trail #3 (https://entire.com/gh/filadd/-/trails/3). Work them in this order:
1. **La marca en la base y el contrato.** Migration `0004_featured_session` with `featured`, `featured_questions` and the partial unique index. `SessionSummary` and `SessionChange` add `featured` and `featuredQuestions`; errors add `NotFeatured` (409). The changelog adds `questions-opened`, with its label, line and color.
2. **Batches que cruzan stores.** The core adds the `Write` type and the `Batch` port; `Repository` adds `writes`. `repositoryOf` builds `writes` from its `statements`, `D1Batch` implements the port, `worker.ts` wires it.
3. **Cambiar la destacada (API).** `Sessions.update` builds the leaving of the featured session as above, removes its changelog items and notifies its classroom. `SessionDisabled` and `NotFeatured` as above. Featured questions on/off create and remove `questions-opened`. `Sessions.featured` reads the mark. Tests in a new `featured.test.ts` with its own fixture.
4. **La regla de la destacada en las escrituras (API).** `featuredSession` in the student writes; Activar outside the featured session answers `NotFeatured`; the first vote stops removing `poll-opened`. The fixtures of polls, questions, raised-hands, classroom and announcements mark their featured session; the classroom without a featured session goes in its own file.
5. **Inicio del estudiante (web).** Renames, "Todas las sesiones", `railLook`, `RailNode` `later`, the star, `SessionLinks` `featured`, active polls of the featured session only, `/aula` by the mark, the `sessionSummary` fixture with the two fields.
6. **Panel de preguntas en la card (web).** `FeaturedQuestions` in the `questions` slot of `FeaturedSession`.
7. **Admin de una sesión (web).** `FeaturedSwitch`, `EnableSessionDialog`, `FeaturedEffects`, `useFeaturedSession`, `ConfirmDialog` slots, `EnabledSwitch` modal and confirmation, `useUpdateSession` without optimistic patch on waiting changes, no "Sesión N de M".
8. **Lista de sesiones del profe (web).** `AdminFeatured`, `AdminSessionRail` with `railLook`, star, dashed node for disabled, no numbers.
9. **Activar y Preguntas destacadas en el aula del profe (web).** `PollStateActions` with `isFeatured`, hiding Activar outside the featured session in the tab and the panel; `FeaturedQuestionsSwitch` above the panel's questions.

Each API test file runs on its own D1, and a D1 holds only one featured session: plan the fixtures accordingly (that is why featuring and "no featured session" get their own files).

# Agentic review

Cleans up a change so mahou:human-review spends its attention on judgment instead of on mechanical findings. It reviews for reuse, simplification, efficiency, altitude, and conformance to the conventions the wiki holds.

It does not look for correctness bugs. Those belong to the human pass, where someone can weigh whether the behavior was intended.

## Fixing without asking

`basics` says every decision belongs to the user and every choice goes back to them as a question. This skill is the exception, and it holds inside these bounds:

- It fixes nothing that would change how the change looks or behaves.
- It keeps every mechanism that a settled program design entry, a settled design tree leaf, an explicit user decision or a source on the conventions list chose. A prototype settles how the change looks and behaves, not how it is coded, so the review may change code that does what the prototype's code did in a different way.
- It may create a new file or edit a file the changeset does not touch when the fix reduces complexity or duplication, or otherwise improves the code.
- It leaves everything uncommitted, so the user can read the whole pass with one `git diff` and discard it as a whole.
- It reports every fix and every skip.

A finding whose fix would break any of those becomes a skipped finding in the report, for the user to rule on.

## Step 1: Establish the changeset

Load mahou:changeset for the repositories, the base, and the diff.

Then settle the conventions list, the sources the conventions reviewers check the change against. When the caller passes one, use it as given. When it does not, follow the wiki indexes, global and local, to the entries about the technologies the diff touches, and add the project's `CLAUDE.md` and `.mahou/basics.md` when present. Open every source on the list. Every fix has to follow them.

## Step 2: Dispatch the facet reviewers

Per repository, one reviewer per facet and one conventions reviewer per source on the list, all in a single message so they run together.

| Facet | Agent | Looks for |
|---|---|---|
| Reuse | `mahou:reuse-reviewer` | new code re-implementing something the codebase already has |
| Simplification | `mahou:simplification-reviewer` | redundant or derivable state, copy-paste with variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind |
| Efficiency | `mahou:efficiency-reviewer` | redundant computation, repeated I/O, independent work run sequentially, closures pinning large scopes |
| Altitude | `mahou:altitude-reviewer` | special cases layered on shared infrastructure where the mechanism underneath should generalize instead |
| Conventions | `mahou:conventions-reviewer`, one per source | departures from the one wiki entry or rule file it is given |

Give each one the repository's absolute path, the base, the diff, and the path to write its findings to. Give each conventions reviewer the path of its source as well, and a findings path of its own.

Reviewers write findings to that file and return the path and a count. Nothing comes back in the message body, which truncates long reports and costs a round trip to recover.

Every round spawns fresh reviewers; never resume one from an earlier round. A reviewer that has seen its own last report defends it and repeats what was skipped, and a reviewer resumed per facet only hears about its own fixes, so it can undo what another facet fixed. From the second round on, give every reviewer the ledger (Step 4) as well.

## Step 3: Apply what came back

Read every findings file. Collapse findings that different facets raised about the same line or mechanism, then fix each survivor.

Skip a finding when its fix would change intended behavior, reach outside the bounds above, or when you judge it a false positive. Record the skip with why the reviewer proposed the change, the problem the reviewer saw in the code, and why you skipped the finding. Never argue with it.

Then read every comment the diff adds, yourself, against the project's comments rule: a wiki entry, the project's `CLAUDE.md` or a rule file in the repository. The reviewers do not flag comments. Remove or rewrite every comment the rule does not allow. When the project states no comments rule, say so and leave the comments as they are.

Run the repository's linters and tests afterwards, scoped to the files you touched rather than the whole tree. The project's `CLAUDE.md` usually names the commands; when it does not, detect them from the lockfile or manifest and say which you ran.

## Step 4: Record the round and show it

Keep one ledger per repository at `agentic-review/<repo>.md` in the change's scratch folder. At the end of each round, append a section for the round with every fix applied (file, line, the facet that raised it, what changed) and every skip with its reason, then the linter and test results.

Show the user the round's status: per repository the count of fixes and skips, one line per fix, each skip with its reason, and the checks' result. Then start the next round without waiting for an answer.

## Step 5: Round again, up to three times

Run Step 2 again with fresh reviewers and the ledger. Tell each reviewer:

- Every fix in the ledger is settled. Do not propose reverting or reshaping one, unless the fix itself introduced a problem on your angle; then cite the ledger entry.
- Every skip in the ledger is settled. Do not raise it again.
- Report only what still stands on your angle in the current diff.

When applying the round's findings, drop any finding that reverses a ledger fix or repeats a ledger skip, and record it as dropped in the round's section.

Stop when a round returns no findings that survive, or after the third round, whichever comes first.

## Step 6: Report and hand off

Per repository: what each round fixed, what it skipped, and the linter and test results, with the ledger path. Write each skipped finding so the user can rule on it without asking back: the problem the reviewer saw and why the reviewer proposed the change, then why the review skipped the finding. Everything stays uncommitted.

Then hand off to mahou:human-review.

---
name: "basics"
description: "Foundation for every mahou skill. Carries the philosophy and rules the agent follows when running any mahou skill. Load before running any other mahou skill."
user-invocable: false
---
# Mahou

The agent is the magic: tireless, fast, and exactly as wise as the instructions it is given. The user is the spellcaster. They draw the circle, they provide the mana, they choose the spell, and the agent pours itself into the shape they drew.

No spell casts itself. No skill picks a library, no skill chooses between two designs, no skill guesses what the user meant. The agent brings facts and state; every fork comes back to the spellcaster as a question.

Skills stay small enough that the user can see what each one did and correct it, instead of large enough that they have to trust the outcome.

## Philosophy

Each skill does one job; when a skill needs a second job, it becomes two skills. A skill tells you how to work, while facts about technologies and tools live in the wiki. Nothing is committed unprompted; when work is ready, say so and wait.

## Rules

1. Never use the phrase "load-bearing".
2. **Never decide for the user.** Map the state, then ask. No recommendations, no leaning toward an option, no answering for them. Give a recommendation only when the user asks for one. When a decision has only one plausible answer, because it follows from decisions already settled or from how the code already works, propose that answer with the fact it follows from and ask the user to confirm or correct it, instead of asking the question open.
3. **Report what you found, not what you assume.** When something is missing, say it is missing. Do not fill the gap with a plausible guess.
4. **Never commit or push as a side effect.** A skill whose entire job is committing, invoked directly by the user, is the exception, because that invocation is the consent.
5. **One job.** If the work in front of you has grown a second job, stop and say so rather than quietly doing both.
6. **Never volunteer next steps.** Answer what was asked, then stop. Do not close a report with work the user did not request: no "still outstanding", no "you may also want to", no queue of follow-ups. If something blocks the job in front of you, state it in one line as a fact. Everything else waits until they ask.

## Code

Comments never go inside a structure definition. Object and array literals, payloads, config entries, test fixtures, interface and type property lists, props, parameter lists: a reader scans all of these as a shape, and a comment between two entries breaks the scan. When the rationale is real, it goes above the structure or at the site that consumes the value.

This holds in every repository, whatever the language.

## Referencing code

When a skill's output points at code, it writes the pointer in one form, so every reference reads the same and can be found by searching for `[[`:

| Points at | Form |
|---|---|
| A declaration | `[[path#symbol]]`, qualified when the name is ambiguous: `[[src/store.ts#Store.save]]` |
| A file | `[[path]]` |
| A line range | `[[path#L12-L30]]` |
| Lines as a commit left them | `[[sha:path#L12-L30]]`, or `[[base..head:path#L12-L30]]` for a range of commits |

Paths are relative to the repository's root; when the output spans several repositories, the path starts with the repository's folder name. Prefer a symbol to a line range, because a symbol survives edits above it. Point at a commit once the code is committed and the reference has to keep showing that version. Check every reference against the file before writing it. Something the change will create has no reference yet: name it in plain text.

## Scratch folder

Every artifact a skill produces for the user and keeps between rounds goes under `.scratch/<change-slug>/` in the project's root, never under `/tmp`: a design handoff, a prototype, a draft, a research file. One directory named after the current change, holding the files the skill writes: `handoff.md`, `design.md`, `research.md`, a `prototypes/` folder, a `reports/` folder, a `test-design/` folder, a `spikes/` folder, whatever the skill defines. A skill that reopens a file reopens it from there, so the folder survives compaction, restarts and the next day. Throwaway files that are not to be reused, such as a diagram written only to validate it, may still use `/tmp`.

Skills say "the change's scratch folder" and name only the path inside it.

### Status

The change's scratch folder keeps `status.md`, the tracker of where the change stands. Read it at the start of every skill that works on the change. Update it at the end of the skill, and as soon as an item the file tracks changes during the conversation. The first skill that writes to the scratch folder creates `status.md`.

It holds pointers only. Never copy into it what a file or page it points to already says.

- **Stage**: one line naming the stage the change is in, such as design settled or tasks created, and the stage that comes next.
- **Links**: the external places the change lives in, such as its task in the tracker, its pull requests and the docs notes that record it.
- **Local artifacts**: each file and folder in the scratch folder, with one line on what it holds.
- **Tracking**: one list of what is still open, such as an open item, a pending task or something waiting on someone else. Each item is one line with a pointer to where its detail lives. Edit an item when its state changes and remove it when it is done.

When a skill's flow ends, check the change's scratch folder before stopping. Check that every file and folder in it has its line in `status.md`, that the stage in `status.md` says where the change stands, and that tracking holds only what is still open. Check that every file the skill wrote matches the state the flow ended in, and that no file contradicts what the user settled. Check that every decision the user settled is written in a file in the scratch folder, and not only in the conversation. Fix every file that fails one of these checks, then stop.

## The wiki

Knowledge about technologies and tools, their gotchas and their patterns, lives in mahou:wiki, indexed one level per folder so entries load on demand. Load it now and read its root indexes, global and local, so that you know which topics have entries when they come up in conversation. Read an entry only when the skill you are running says so, or when the user asks for a check against the conventions for a technology. Do not bring an entry's conventions into a question the user has not asked; when a topic with an entry comes up in a decision, say the entry exists and offer to read it.

The wiki is the standard the conventions reviewer measures a change against. mahou:learn writes it.

## The project's docs

Projects mahou runs in keep their own documentation in a folder they own, usually `docs/`. How to find it and what its structure is made of live in mahou:docs, which every skill and agent that reads or writes documentation loads. Skills that do not touch documentation leave it alone.

## The project's invariants

Projects keep the rules that every change respects in an invariants note in their docs folder. The rules cover how the product behaves and how the system is built. Before any decision or proposal, read the docs folder's index, find the invariants note in it, and read the note. Check every decision and proposal against it. When a decision would break a rule in the note, say so in the question that settles the decision and name the rule.

## The local layer

A project can change how a skill behaves in a `.mahou/` folder at its root: `.mahou/basics.md` for standing rules, `.mahou/<skill>.md` for one skill, `.mahou/wiki/` for local knowledge. Every skill reads its own file when present, and local wins over global when the two conflict.

# Changeset

Defines the change once, so every skill that reasons about one agrees on what it is. A skill that reviews, traces, or reports on a change loads this first.

## Address every repository by path

Collect the absolute path of every repository the change touches. Use `git -C <repo-path>` for every git command and absolute paths for every read.

**Never `cd`.** A foreground `cd` persists across Bash calls, so a later call, especially one of several sent in the same message, runs in whichever repository was entered last and returns its output under the wrong name. Nothing errors, and the output looks plausible.

## Establish the base

The base is the commit you measure the change against. Report it, never assume it silently.

```
bash ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/skills/changeset/scripts/find-base-branch.sh <repo-path>
```

The script fetches and returns, as JSON, the remote branch that the current branch has the fewest commits ahead of. That remote branch is the one the current branch was cut from. It skips the branch's own remote copy. Use its `base_branch` as `origin/<base_branch>`. Do not take the base from `origin/HEAD`, because it can point at a trunk the work did not branch from. When the script errors or returns a branch you cannot account for, ask. **Never guess between `main` and `master`** by checking which exists, because a repository can carry both. Do not fall back to `HEAD~1`.

Two sources reviewing the same work against different bases produce findings you cannot compare. When more than one source is involved, report each one's base.

## Compose the diff

A changeset is composed from these parts, and you decide which are in scope rather than taking a default:

| Part | Command |
|---|---|
| Committed on the branch | `git -C <repo> diff <base>...HEAD` |
| Uncommitted | `git -C <repo> diff HEAD` |
| Untracked | `git -C <repo> status --porcelain` |

Use the three-dot form for the committed part. It shows what the branch added since it diverged and excludes anything that landed on the base meanwhile. Two-dot mixes the two and attributes other people's commits to this change.

Stashed work is not part of the changeset. Neither is work on another branch. Include either only when the user says to, and say in the report that you did.

State the composition you used in one line before presenting anything derived from it, so a wrong scope shows up instead of passing unnoticed.

## Separate introduced from pre-existing

A line inside the diff is not necessarily a change the diff made. Before calling anything introduced, read the base version:

```
git -C <repo-path> show <base>:<path>
```

Compare the behavior, not the text. Code can move, be re-indented, or be extracted without changing what it does, and a symbol can sit untouched while its callers change what they pass it. `git log` and `git show <commit>` settle which commit introduced a line when the base comparison is not enough.

Every claim that something is new, changed, or broken carries this distinction: introduced here, pre-existing, or pre-existing and widened by this change.

description: Delegate work by spawning another agent as a herdr tab.
---
# The herdr-subagents protocol

What you follow as a parent agent driving herdr subagents. You drive every exchange: you prompt, your children reply.

## Your prompts — `<supervisor-agent>`

Wrap every prompt you send to a child in `<supervisor-agent>…</supervisor-agent>`. The tag is how the child tells your directive from a human steering it directly — an untagged message reaching the child means a human has taken over that tab.

## Your child's questions — `<subagent-ask>`

A child that needs a decision ends its turn with the question wrapped in `<subagent-ask>…</subagent-ask>`. When you collect, that tag is your discriminator: present means the child is asking you something (reply, and do not close the tab); absent means the message is the child's result.

## Invoking delegation

The delegate skill is invoked as `/skill:delegate` on pi and `/delegate` on claude. A child invokes it on its own harness. If you direct a cross-harness child to delegate, name the form for its harness in your prompt.

When a message carries a skill invocation (any `/skill:...` or `/...` command), it comes **first, outside the `<supervisor-agent>` tag** — it is a harness command, not part of the tagged payload. The command and the opening tag share the first line, space-separated: `/skill:implement <supervisor-agent>...`. This holds for every skill, not only delegation: a parent directing a child to run `/skill:implement`, `/skill:tdd`, or any other skill prefixes the command before the tag on the same line.

---

# Delegate

You drive subagents through a single interface that wraps herdr. It handles the fragile parts — verifying the spawn landed, confirming the prompt was delivered, tracking pane and tab ids — so you treat each command as trustworthy and act on what it reports.

Use the `subagent` tool for all delegation commands. Pass `command` and the relevant `options`:

| command  | options                                           |
| -------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| spawn    | `{ kind, agent?, label, model?, body?, body_file?, worktree?, branch?, base? }` |
| prompt   | `{ pane_id, body | body_file }`                               |
| wait     | `{ pane_id, timeout? }`                           |
| collect  | `{ pane_id }`                                     |
| close    | `{ tab_id }`                                      |
| list     | `{}`                                              |
| read     | `{ pane_id, lines? }`                             |
| unblock  | `{ pane_id, keys }`                               |

`wait` is rarely needed — your session auto-wakes you when a child finishes.

All children are herdr tabs. One tab, one task. A child lives in your workspace unless you give it a worktree, which puts it in a workspace of its own.

## When to delegate

Delegate when the work is genuinely separable and worth a tab of its own. Prefer breadth — several children at your own level — over deep chains. Close your children before spawning the next batch.

Label each tab after the work it is doing; a workspace of labelled tabs is your fleet view.

## Spawn

- `kind` is required and never self-detected. Your default is your own harness; pass the other only when the work or the caller explicitly asks for it. Only `pi` and `claude` are supported.
- `agent` is optional. Omit it to dispatch a generic child running the harness's default agent (it still receives the herdr onboarding). When given, it is a name defined in the project's agent files, never a path — and the name is all you provide: the child's system prompt is applied from the definition at spawn, so never paste the definition into the prompt nor direct the child to read it.
- `model` is optional. Omitted, the child runs its harness's default model. It is a model name of the child's harness, passed through verbatim, so what is valid depends on `kind`. A bare id that more than one provider carries is ambiguous — pi exits on it and the spawn fails — so qualify it with the provider, such as `zai/glm-5.3-flash`. When you spawn without a model named by the work or the caller, pick one yourself: judge the task's difficulty and choose the cheapest model available that can solve it. Reach for a heavier model only when the work needs the capability — mechanical tasks never do.
- `body` is optional. Given, the task is delivered with the spawn — one call instead of spawn-then-prompt. Wrap it in `<supervisor-agent>…</supervisor-agent>` exactly as you would with `prompt`; delivery is verified the same way. Every message after it goes through `prompt`. Pass it as text, or through `body_file` with a path to a file whose content is exactly the body (absolute, or relative to the cwd).
- The label is final; a child never renames its own tab.

Returns the new child's `pane_id` and `tab_id`. Keep both — you prompt and collect by `pane_id`, and close by `tab_id`. If spawn fails, the half-created tab is closed and the failure is reported; surface that to the human rather than retrying blindly. Two failures are different: `blocked` means the child came up on a startup dialog and never became ready. It is alive, so its tab is kept and its pane comes back with the dialog on it — see **Blocked children**. And a spawn with `body` can fail at delivery: the child is alive and tracked, and the failure names its `pane_id` — retry with `prompt`.

## Worktrees

`worktree` gives a child its own checkout on its own branch, in its own herdr workspace, instead of sharing your working directory.

Use it when the child will **write** — implementing, refactoring, fixing a bug — and above all when several children write at once. Sharing one checkout means they overwrite each other's edits and fight over the same branch.

It is not the default. Research, planning, design, review — anything answered by reading — belongs in your own checkout, where the child sees the code you actually have and leaves nothing behind. A single child making changes is usually fine without one too; isolation pays off when there is something to isolate from.

- `branch` names the branch. A new name creates a worktree; an existing one joins it.
- `base` is what a new branch forks from. Omitted, your current HEAD.
- Nothing else changes. You prompt, collect, and close a worktree child exactly like any other.

Several children can share one worktree. Point a second child at an existing branch and it lands in the same checkout alongside the first — that is how you put a reviewer on another child's work, or hand a branch from one child to the next. Children sharing a checkout see each other's edits, so give them non-overlapping work, or run them one after another.

Close children as you always do. A worktree outlives its children until the last one goes, and closing that last child takes the checkout with it — so a sibling still working there is never disturbed. The branch always survives: name it when you report a child's result, or the work is lost to whoever reads the report.

Uncommitted changes are never discarded. If the last child's checkout is dirty, the close reports that and the child stays open — prompt it to commit, then close it again.

## Prompt

Wrap **every** prompt you send to a child in `<supervisor-agent>…</supervisor-agent>`. Tagging is what tells the child it is a supervisor directive rather than a human steering it. The first prompt can ride `spawn`'s `body`; `prompt` is for every message after it. Either takes the body as text or through a file path (`body_file`); the file's content is exactly the body, tag included.

Delivery is verified: the interface watches for the child to act on the prompt and resends if the first send is dropped. A child that is already `working` receives the prompt as a steer — no state change follows a steer, so the accepted submission itself is the receipt and the message is never resent.

When a child needs you, your session wakes you automatically, so you never arm a wake yourself: a finished turn (`done`, or an `idle` that ends a turn) wakes you to collect, `blocked` wakes you to surface the dialog to the human, the resume from a block wakes you so you know they answered, and a lost child (`gone`) wakes you too.

## Blocked children

`blocked` is herdr recognising a dialog on a child's screen — a tool approval, a question it opened instead of asking you, a startup trust prompt. It is neither terminal nor a failure: the child is alive and one keypress from carrying on. It is also the state most in need of you, because unlike a finished turn it will never resolve on its own.

A blocked child wakes you. What you do with it:

- `read` its pane to see what is being asked. This is the one screen read in the interface; it is for a blocked child, not for checking progress.
- **Tell the human what it needs and which tab to answer it in** — name the tab label and the pane id. The answer is theirs to give, not yours: you cannot know whether a permission prompt should be granted, and a question the child asked is a question for a person.
- You are woken again when the child resumes, so you can carry on without watching the tab.

`unblock` sends key presses (`enter`, `esc`, `1 enter`) and reports whether the block cleared. Use it **only when the human has explicitly told you to answer that dialog** — "yes, accept it" is your authorization, and it saves them a tab switch. Never on your own judgement, and never as a way to keep a child moving. It refuses a child that is not blocked: keys sent to an idle child are typed into its prompt box and corrupt its next prompt.

A child that asks through a dialog rather than `<subagent-ask>` has misrouted its question — surface it, and prompt it to use the tag next time. Whoever answers a dialog, the child cannot tell you from the human.

## Collect

When a child finishes, you are woken to collect it.

Returns `{pane_id, label, agent, status, message?, error?}`. `status` reflects herdr's state, **not** task success — a child that gives up still reaches `done`. Read `message` and judge the result yourself.

The `<subagent-ask>…</subagent-ask>` tag in the child's final message marks a question for you rather than a result.

`blocked` is non-terminal: the child is waiting, not finished. See **Blocked children**.

Once you no longer need a child, you can close it.

## Close

Close a child once you have its result and no longer need it. Closing before spawning the next batch keeps the fleet clean. The timing is a delegation question, not a results question: keep a child open because a fix round is coming, close it when nothing more will be delegated to it.

## The fleet

Run `list` to see every tracked child and its status. A wake can be missed; `list` is the durable backstop you run on demand, so a missed wake is never fatal. Run it whenever you are unsure what is outstanding.

# D1: SQLite on Cloudflare, migrations and drivers

verified: 2026-10-04

Answers what D1 offers as a database, how it is reached, how its schema is migrated, and whether SQLAlchemy and Alembic can drive it. Distilled from documentation and package inspection while weighing a Postgres-to-D1 move; nothing was run against D1.

## Knowledge

- D1 runs on SQLite's engine with the JSON extension, FTS5 and math functions. `PRAGMA foreign_keys` and `defer_foreign_keys` are available. `run()` returns `meta.changes`, so a conditional `UPDATE ... WHERE status = ...` can be checked by its row count. `batch()` runs its statements as one transaction.
- Limits on Paid: 10 GB per database (500 MB on Free), 2 MB per row or value, 100 bound parameters per query, 1,000 queries per Worker invocation. Each database is single-threaded.
- Pricing on Paid includes 25 billion rows read, 50 million rows written and 5 GB a month; beyond that $0.001 per million reads, $1.00 per million writes and $0.75 per GB-month. No egress charges.
- From a Worker it is a binding. From anything else, such as a container, the only documented route is the REST API.
- Migrations are hand-written `.sql` files in a `migrations/` folder, created with `wrangler d1 migrations create`, applied with `--local` or `--remote`, and tracked in a `d1_migrations` table. There is no down migration: a failing migration rolls back itself and the earlier ones stay. Time Travel keeps 30 days of point-in-time restore on Paid (7 on Free).
- Read replication is GA at no cost; without the Sessions API every query goes to the primary, and with it reads are sequentially consistent.
- `sqlalchemy-cloudflare-d1` (0.4.1, 2026-10-02) connects over the REST API or a Python Worker binding. Its async engine is unavailable inside Workers, its `commit` and `rollback` are no-ops because every statement auto-commits, and its package contains no Alembic support. No other package connects Alembic to D1; Alembic's offline `--sql` output written into D1's migration files is an untested route.

# kurasu: checks and tests

verified: 2026-11-02

Answers which checks reject code in kurasu and where its tests live.

## Knowledge

- oxlint runs type-aware with every rule as an error; oxfmt formats the code.
- A local plugin enforces boundaries: `apps/web` imports only `@kurasu/contract` and `@kurasu/slides` among the project's packages; `packages/core` imports no Cloudflare, Alchemy, Drizzle or jose; `packages/*` never import `apps/*`.
- TypeScript rules: `== null` instead of `=== null` or `=== undefined`; no enums (a const map and a derived type); named exports only.
- The tsconfig compiles with `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`: an optional prop `?: T` rejects an explicit `undefined`. A prop every caller writes is required and typed `T | undefined`; a prop callers may omit is `?: T | undefined`.
- React rules: arrow-function components with a `Props` interface; React imported by name; conditional rendering with a ternary, never `&&`; no nested ternaries; one component per file; no destructured `useQuery` or `useMutation`.
- The project copies anti-slop into `tools/oxlint/anti-slop/` and adapts it as its own, with its generic and Effect rules.
- `@effect/tsgo` makes `tsc` fail on Effect diagnostics: missing services, `any` in error channels, global `Date`, `fetch` or `console` inside Effect.
- lefthook runs check on every commit; nobody commits with `--no-verify`. The tests run by hand with `pnpm test` before handing work over, because the API suite takes about a minute. turbo caches each package's tests until the package or one of its workspace dependencies changes.
- Tests are integration tests only, in `apps/api/test` (Alchemy's `alchemy/Test/Vitest` in dev mode, HTTP and WebSocket against the local stack) and `apps/web/test` (screens with the real router, the API answered by MSW, Testing Library on happy-dom). Tests live only there: the `test-location` lint rule rejects a test file anywhere else, and the root `projects` list names only the two apps. Before a package whose logic is too complex to cover through the API or the web gets its own tests, extend both the `test-location` rule and the root `projects` list to include it. Tests do not mock modules.
- Two web test helpers control when the mock server answers a request and what it answers. `heldResponse(method, path)` (`test/helpers/held-response.ts`) holds every request to the path until the test calls `release`, so the test can check the screen while the request is still waiting: a skeleton, a pending button. Released without a response, the requests fall through to the handlers already in place. `failingRoute(method, path, status = 500)` (`test/helpers/failing-route.ts`) answers the path with that status and a body no endpoint declares, as a failing server does.
- Pass the handlers that replace the page's own as the `overrides` argument of the test file's `openPage`, which calls `server.use` with them after the page's handlers and before the page renders. If the test calls `server.use` after the page opens, the requests that the page sends while it loads have already reached the page's handlers.

# Commit changes

Commits the changes done to this repository using conventional commits (https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/). This is the one skill whose job is committing, so the user asking for it, or a skill reaching a commit step the user approved, is the consent `basics` asks for. Pushing is not part of the job.

## Message format

```
<type>[optional scope]: <description>

[optional body]

[optional footer(s)]
```

Types:

- **fix**: patches a bug (PATCH in semantic versioning)
- **feat**: introduces a feature (MINOR)
- A `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer marks a breaking change (MAJOR) and can go on a commit of any type. Never use the `!` after the type or scope for this.
- **build**, **chore**, **ci**, **docs**, **style**, **refactor**, **perf**, **test**, with their usual meanings from `@commitlint/config-conventional`.

Footers other than `BREAKING CHANGE: <description>` follow the git trailer format.

## Procedure

1. **Analyze the repository state.** `git status` for everything modified, added and deleted; `git diff` for the nature of each change; `git diff --staged` for anything already staged. When the project has a `CLAUDE.md` or a `.mahou/commit-changes.md` that names a scope convention or a commit convention of its own, read it and follow it.

2. **Plan the groups.** Group by logical relationship: same feature, same fix, same area. Tests, type definitions and directly related changes go with the main change. Never mix unrelated changes in one commit. Refactors go in their own commit unless small and tightly coupled to the main change.

3. **Present the groups and wait.** Always, even when there is one group and it looks obvious. Show every group with its proposed message and its file list, then ask how to proceed: with one group, proceed or split further; with several, proceed or merge. Take the user's regrouping literally.

4. **Commit each approved group.** Stage only that group's files with `git add <file>...`, then commit with the agreed message. Never `git add -A` or `git add .`; an untracked file the user did not mention is not part of any group until they say so.

   A file whose changes belong to two groups is split by hunk. The file appears under both groups with a word on which change goes where. To stage one side, write the file's diff to a temporary patch with `git diff <file> > /tmp/<name>.diff`, delete the hunks that belong to the other group while keeping the diff header, and apply it with `git apply --cached /tmp/<name>.diff`. Once that group is committed, the hunks left in the working tree are what `git add <file>` stages for the other. `git add -p` is interactive and does not run here.

## Message rules

- Description in the imperative, present tense: "add", not "added" or "adding". Short, no trailing period.
- The message says **what** the change does, never why it was made or where the request came from. "fix(auth): add null check for expired tokens", never "fix: address PR comments".
- A body, when needed, is simple and direct: no file listings, no implementation walkthrough, no test section.
- **Scope** is the area of the project the change touches: the top-level module, directory, package or service name, one or two lowercase words. Check `git log` for the scopes the project already uses and reuse them. When the change spans areas, use the primary one; when nothing dominates, omit the scope.

## When something is off

- No changes: say so and stop.
- Merge conflict markers in the tree: say so and stop; nothing is committed over a conflict.
- Untracked files: ask whether they belong in a group before staging them.

# Agentic review report: kurasu (`app/`)

All three rounds ran: 26 fixes and 18 skips. The fixes are committed in eight commits on `feat/preguntas-en-la-card`, nothing is pushed, and `pnpm run check` and `pnpm test` pass. None of the fixes changes how the app looks or behaves.

The changeset was the branch measured against `d09d518` (`git diff d09d518...HEAD`), plus each round's uncommitted fixes. The ledger is at `/home/agus/workspace/filadd/agentic-engineering-famaf-extension-course/.scratch/preguntas-en-la-card/reports/review/ledger.md`.

**Reviewers.** Each round had 14 fresh reviewers on Sonnet 5.5:
- four facets: reuse, simplification, efficiency, altitude;
- one conventions reviewer per source: `app/AGENTS.md`, your style file, the local wiki entries `architecture`, `api`, `web`, `fence` and `alchemy/local-tests`, and the global entries `naming/booleans`, `react/component-modules` and `tanstack-query/operation-hooks`.

The auto-mode classifier rate-limited (429) a few spawns and one batch read. Each was retried and ran, and no reviewer was skipped.

**Rounds.**

| Round | Findings | Fixes | Skips |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 46 | 15 | 11 |
| 2 | 12 | 7 | 2 |
| 3 | 9 | 4 | 5 |

The review stopped at round 3, the skill's limit, not because the reviewers ran out of findings.

## Fixes and their commits

**`044a280` refactor(api): run the featured session's leaving in one helper and name the deferred writes once**
- **1, 16, 17.** `Sessions.update` checked `Option.isSome(leaving)` three times, read the featured session on every update, and did a second `store.get` on the plain path. Now:
  - one `updateLeaving` helper holds the whole leaving path, and its read-back uses `existingSession`;
  - `featured()` runs only when `change.featured === true`;
  - the plain path uses the row `store.update` returns, as the base did;
  - `leavingOf` returns only the id.
- **2.** The `Writes` comment had pushed the `Repository` doc comment off its type; each type has its own comment again.
- **3.** `repositoryOf` returned the same object as both `statements` and `writes`. It is now only `writes`, and `codes`, `materials` and `users` use that name.
- **4.** `polls.isFeatured` re-read the session itself; it is now built on `featuredSession`.
- **14 (part).** Removed the narrative comment above `leavingOf` and rewrapped the long `Sessions` comment.

**`5eddd62` test(api): raise the hand each raised-hands test lowers**
- **22.** Ana's seeded hand made "raising the hand…" pass whether or not the request created a hand, and the lowering test depended on what earlier tests left. The fixture drops that hand, and the lowering test raises the hand it lowers.

**`253abbe` refactor(web): draw the session rail node in one component**
- **5, 18.** Both rails drew the same check and star node. That is now one `SessionRailNode`. The look names are listed once, in `RailNodeLook`, and `RailLook` is derived from it.

**`1b5d4d3` refactor(web): share the switch button, row class, error text and warning colours of the session switches**
- **6.** The four new switch buttons share `ui/SwitchButton`.
- **7.** `FeaturedSwitch` picks its confirmation once with `confirmationOf`, instead of three overlapping branches.
- **11.** The warning's hex colours are now the theme colours `blush` and `wine`, with the same values.
- **12.** `EnabledSwitch` and `EnableSessionDialog` are an `EnabledSwitch/` module folder with an `index.ts`.
- **19.** "No se pudo guardar el cambio…" is one `updateErrorText`.
- **20.** `renderTrigger={toggle}` replaces a lambda that only forwarded its argument.
- **24.** The local `enabled` is now `isEnabled`.
- **26.** A `switch-row` class replaces the repeated row utility classes.
- **14 (part).** Removed the narrative comment above `EnabledSwitch`.

**`acb4683` refactor(web): build count labels with one helper**
- **8.** One `ui/count-label.ts` replaces two local copies, and `answers` is built on it.
- **9.** The nested ternaries in JSX became `pollsLine`, `handsLine` and `toggleLabel`. The `FeaturedEffects` skeleton takes its text from the same builders.
- **14 (part).** Removed the narrative comment above `FeaturedQuestions`.

**`58d957e` refactor(web): find the featured session with one helper**
- **10, 23.** One `findFeatured`, which accepts `undefined`, is used by `useFeaturedSession` and the three routes.
- **14 (part).** Removed the narrative comments above `useFeaturedSession` and `railLook`, and rewrapped the long lines in `routes/_app/index.tsx`.

**`af1a155` refactor(web): accept undefined in the optional emptyText and confirmIcon props**
- **13.** `emptyText` and `confirmIcon` are typed `?: T | undefined`, as `fence.md` requires for props callers may omit.

**`6f275af` test(web): name the boolean helper parameters with is**
- **15, 21, 25.** `isOtherFeaturedQuestions`, `isFeatured` (two helpers) and `isWithQuestions`.

## Skipped findings

For each skip: what the reviewer saw and proposed, then why the review left it.

1. **`FeaturedQuestions` repeats `StudentQuestions`** (reuse, altitude).
   - Reviewer: both have the same query, vote sort, skeleton and row renderers and will drift apart. Proposed a shared piece or a limit option on `StudentQuestions`.
   - Skipped: the program design keeps `FeaturedQuestions` as its own component, because `StudentQuestions` shows the whole list unfolded with the form as its header.

2. **`isFeatured` is passed through six poll components** (reuse, simplification).
   - Reviewer: one boolean goes down four levels next to the existing `canActivate`. Proposed folding the two together.
   - Skipped: the brief has `PollStateActions` take `isFeatured` and hide Activar. `canActivate` disables the button instead, so merging them changes the screen.

3. **`useFeaturedSession` and the `select` type parameter in the API layer** (simplification).
   - Reviewer: generic plumbing for one call site. Proposed `.find` inside `ContentTab`.
   - Skipped: the program design chose this hook, a module-level `select`, at your request.

4. **`useUpdateSession` invalidates polls and raised hands on every update** (efficiency).
   - Reviewer: title edits and the featured-questions switch trigger refetches that cannot change anything. Proposed building the invalidation list from the change.
   - Skipped: the brief fixes this invalidation set, and a per-change list would change what the screen refetches.

5. **The core's `Write` type is shaped by Drizzle (`toSQL`)** (wiki-architecture).
   - Reviewer: the adapter's shape leaks into a core port. Proposed a branded opaque type that `packages/database` builds and unwraps.
   - Skipped: it reshapes the port settled in Q2 and needs a cast or wrapper in the adapter. This one is for you to decide.

6. **The tests in `featured.test.ts` depend on their order** (wiki-local-tests).
   - Reviewer: each test starts from the featured session the previous one left. Proposed one file per scenario, or a reset at the start of each test.
   - Skipped: the brief and the test design put featuring in one file, because a D1 holds only one featured session.

7. **The A41 test in `changelog.test.ts` has to run last** (wiki-local-tests).
   - Reviewer: it relies on running last and is kept correct only by a comment. Proposed moving it to `featured.test.ts`.
   - Skipped: the test design places row A41 in `changelog.test.ts`.

8. **`SessionLinks` prop `featured` has no `is`** (naming-booleans).
   - Reviewer: proposed renaming it `isFeatured`.
   - Skipped: the program design (Q3) names the prop `featured`.

9. **`openQuestions({ featured, featuredQuestions })` in `admin-classroom.test.tsx`** (naming-booleans).
   - Reviewer: booleans without `is`, flagged as borderline.
   - Skipped as a false positive: the object is spread into a `Session`, so its keys are the session's field names.

10. **`leavingOf` and `lineOf` should be in their own modules** (user-style).
    - Reviewer: cited the one-function-per-module rule.
    - Skipped: each has one caller in its file, the rule allows high cohesion, and the reviewer itself called keeping them defensible.

11. **The `FeaturedEffects` skeleton should be the real list with example data** (wiki-web).
    - Reviewer: the skeleton is a hand-written list.
    - Skipped: `.skeleton` only paints `skeleton-block` elements, so the real list without them would draw an empty skeleton. That changes how loading looks.

12. **`FeaturedQuestionsSwitch` uses `text-coal` and `border-sand` on the classroom panel** (wiki-web).
    - Reviewer: the panel turns dark in dark mode, where this text cannot be read. Proposed theme colours or a `bg-paper` card.
    - Skipped: either fix changes how the switch looks, and the colours come from the prototype. Dark mode is for you to decide.

13. **The featured-questions switch renders nothing while the session loads** (wiki-web).
    - Reviewer: it appears late and pushes the questions down. Proposed a skeleton.
    - Skipped: a skeleton changes how loading looks.

14. **The admin rail gets `featuredPosition` and searches the list again for the id** (simplification, altitude).
    - Reviewer: the route turns the featured session into a position and the rail turns it back. Proposed passing the session itself.
    - Skipped: the program design (Q3) chose `featuredPosition`.

15. **The not-featured note is placed by two different rules in the polls tab and the panel** (altitude).
    - Reviewer: proposed one rule for both.
    - Skipped: placing it under the last draft is validation fix `ee83edd` (row B39), and a single rule would move the note.

16. **`usePolls({ sessionId: featured?.id ?? "" })` uses an empty string as a placeholder** (simplification).
    - Reviewer: the types accept an id that must never reach the API. Proposed a hook that owns the guard.
    - Skipped: the guard sits in the same call, and a new module for one call site was judged not worth it.

17. **`FeaturedQuestions` wraps only its list in a skeleton, not the whole card** (wiki-web).
    - Reviewer: the rule is to wrap a whole card, never its inside.
    - Skipped: the change alters how the validated card looks while loading.

18. **`FeaturedQuestionsSwitch` repeats the question row's card classes** (wiki-web, low severity).
    - Reviewer: proposed a shared class.
    - Skipped: only `rounded-[14px] border-[1.5px] border-sand` is shared, and the colours fall under skip 12.
